lesson.summary: Variables are created by assignment — no declaration needed. Core types: int, float, complex, str, bool, None, plus list, tuple, dict and set. Operators: + - * / (true division) // (floor division) % (remainder) ** (power). `and`/`or` return one of their operands; comparisons can be chained (1 < x < 10).
lesson.code:
name = "Ada"        # str
age = 36            # int
pi = 3.14           # float
ok = True           # bool
print(7 / 2, 7 // 2, 7 % 2, 2 ** 3)   # 3.5 3 1 8
print(type(pi).__name__)              # float
print(int("12") + 3, str(5) + "5")    # 15 55

lesson.summary: Strings are IMMUTABLE sequences of characters. Index with s[0] / s[-1], slice with s[start:stop:step] (stop excluded). Methods return NEW strings: upper, lower, title, capitalize, swapcase, strip, replace, split, join, find/index, count, startswith/endswith, isdigit/isalpha/…, center/ljust/rjust/zfill, partition, removeprefix/removesuffix.
lesson.code:
s = "  Hello World  "
print(s.strip())            # "Hello World"
print(s.lower().count("o")) # 2
t = "python"
print(t[0], t[-1], t[1:4])  # p n yth
print(t[::-1])              # nohtyp
print("-".join("a b c".split()))  # a-b-c

lesson.summary: Lists are ordered and MUTABLE. Methods change the list in place (and return None): append, extend, insert, remove, pop, clear, sort, reverse; index and count search it; copy makes a shallow copy. Built-ins: len, sum, min, max, sorted, reversed, enumerate, zip, any, all. Comprehensions: [expr for x in it if cond].
lesson.code:
nums = [3, 1, 4]
nums.append(1)        # [3, 1, 4, 1]
nums.insert(0, 9)     # [9, 3, 1, 4, 1]
nums.remove(1)        # [9, 3, 4, 1]
last = nums.pop()     # 1 → [9, 3, 4]
print(sorted(nums), nums.index(4))
print([x * 2 for x in nums if x > 3])

lesson.summary: Tuples are ordered and IMMUTABLE — created with commas: t = (1, 2, 3) or t = 1, 2, 3. A single-item tuple needs a trailing comma: (5,). Only two methods: count() and index(). They support indexing, slicing, +, *, in, unpacking (a, *rest = t), and — being hashable — can be dict keys.
lesson.code:
t = (10, 20, 30, 20)
print(t[1], t[-1], t[1:3])   # 20 20 (20, 30)
print(t.count(20), t.index(30))  # 2 2
a, *rest = t                 # a=10, rest=[20, 30, 20]
print(type((5)).__name__, type((5,)).__name__)  # int tuple
# t[0] = 1  → TypeError

lesson.summary: A dict maps unique, hashable KEYS to values and keeps insertion order. d[k] reads (KeyError if missing) — d.get(k, default) is safe. Methods: keys, values, items, update, pop, popitem, setdefault, clear, copy, fromkeys. `in` checks keys. Comprehension: {k: v for …}.
lesson.code:
ages = {"Asha": 21, "Ravi": 25}
ages["Neha"] = 23          # add
ages["Asha"] = 22          # update
print(ages.get("Dev", 0))  # 0
print(list(ages.keys()))   # ['Asha', 'Ravi', 'Neha']
for name, age in ages.items():
    print(name, age)

lesson.summary: A set is an UNORDERED collection of UNIQUE, hashable items: {1, 2, 3} or set(iterable) — {} is an empty dict! Methods: add, update, remove (KeyError if missing), discard (safe), pop, clear, union |, intersection &, difference -, symmetric_difference ^, issubset <=, issuperset >=, isdisjoint. frozenset is the immutable version.

lesson.summary: if / elif / else run the FIRST branch whose condition is true. Combine conditions with and / or / not (short-circuit). Nest ifs for dependent checks. One-line choice: a if cond else b. match/case (3.10+) compares a value against patterns. Falsy values: 0, 0.0, "", [], {}, (), None, False.

`for` iterates over any iterable (range, str, list, dict…). range(start, stop, step) excludes stop. `while` repeats while a condition is true. `break` exits, `continue` skips to the next iteration, and a loop's `else` runs only if no break happened. Nested loops multiply the work.
lesson.code:
for i in range(1, 10, 3):
    print(i, end=" ")      # 1 4 7
n = 1234
total = 0
while n > 0:
    total += n % 10
    n //= 10
print(total)               # 10

lesson.summary: Pattern programs train nested-loop thinking. The OUTER loop picks the row; INNER loops (or string repetition like "*" * k) print the spaces and characters for that row. Classic shapes: right triangle, pyramid, inverted pyramid, diamond, hourglass, rhombus, butterfly, rainbow (arch), heart, hollow square, number & alphabet triangles.
lesson.code:
n = 3
for i in range(1, n + 1):          # butterfly — top half
    print("*" * i + " " * (2 * (n - i)) + "*" * i)
for i in range(n, 0, -1):          # bottom half
    print("*" * i + " " * (2 * (n - i)) + "*" * i)

lesson.summary: Types of functions: BUILT-IN (len, print…), USER-DEFINED (def), LAMBDA (anonymous one-liners), RECURSIVE (call themselves), HIGHER-ORDER (take/return functions: map, filter, sorted(key=)), NESTED & CLOSURES, GENERATORS (yield) and DECORATORS (@wrap). Parameters: positional, keyword, default, *args (tuple), **kwargs (dict). Scope follows LEGB; use global/nonlocal to assign outer variables.
lesson.code:
def power(base, exp=2):          # default parameter
    return base ** exp

square = lambda x: x * x         # lambda
print(power(3), power(2, 5))     # 9 32
print(list(map(square, [1, 2, 3])))   # [1, 4, 9]

def gen(n):                      # generator
    for i in range(n):
        yield i

lesson.summary: A recursive function calls itself on a smaller input until it reaches a BASE CASE. Types: direct, indirect (mutual), tail (call is last), head (call first), linear (one call), tree (several calls, e.g. Fibonacci) and nested (a call inside the argument: f(f(n))). Deep recursion raises RecursionError (~1000 frames); memoize repeated calls with functools.lru_cache.

Declare with const (default) or let (reassignable); avoid var (function-scoped, hoisted). Types: number, bigint, string, boolean, undefined, null, symbol, object. + with a string concatenates, other math operators convert to numbers. Use === (strict) rather than ==. Math has round, floor, ceil, trunc, max, min, abs, pow, sqrt.

Strings are immutable. Read characters with s[i] or s.at(-1). Methods return new strings: toUpperCase, toLowerCase, trim, slice, substring, indexOf, includes, startsWith, endsWith, replace (first match), replaceAll, split, repeat, padStart, padEnd, charAt, charCodeAt, concat. Template literals: `Hi ${name}`.

lesson.summary: Arrays are ordered lists. Mutating methods: push, pop, shift, unshift, splice, sort, reverse, fill. Non-mutating: slice, concat, map, filter, reduce, find, findIndex, some, every, includes, indexOf, join, flat. sort() compares strings by default — pass (a, b) => a - b for numbers.
lesson.code:
const nums = [5, 1, 10];
nums.push(3);                           // [5, 1, 10, 3]
console.log(nums.map(n => n * 2));      // [10, 2, 20, 6]
console.log(nums.filter(n => n > 2));   // [5, 10, 3]
console.log(nums.reduce((a, b) => a + b, 0)); // 19
nums.sort((a, b) => a - b);             // [1, 3, 5, 10]

lesson.summary: Objects store key–value properties. Read with obj.key or obj[key]; missing properties are undefined. Add, change and delete freely (even with const). Object.keys/values/entries, Object.assign, spread {...obj} (shallow copy), destructuring { a, b: renamed, c = default }, JSON.stringify/parse, optional chaining ?.

Set: unique values in insertion order — add, has, delete, size, clear; [...new Set(arr)] removes duplicates. Map: key → value pairs where keys can be ANY type — set, get, has, delete, size, keys(), values(), entries(). Both are iterable with for...of.

if / else if / else run the first matching branch. switch compares one value against cases — remember break, or execution falls through. Ternary: cond ? a : b. Logical operators && || ! short-circuit; ?? provides defaults for null/undefined. Falsy values: false, 0, "", null, undefined, NaN.
for (init; condition; update), while, do...while (runs at least once), for...of (values of arrays/strings/Sets/Maps) and for...in (keys of objects). break exits, continue skips to the next iteration.

Build each row as a string, then console.log it: " ".repeat(n - i) + "*".repeat(2 * i - 1). The outer loop picks the row, the inner loops (or repeat) fill it. Shapes: triangles, pyramids, diamond, hourglass, rhombus, butterfly, rainbow, heart, hollow square, number/alphabet triangles.

Types: function DECLARATION (hoisted), function EXPRESSION, ARROW function (=>, no own this), IIFE, CALLBACK, HIGHER-ORDER (takes/returns functions), CLOSURE, GENERATOR (function*), ASYNC, RECURSIVE. Parameters can have defaults (used for undefined) and ...rest. Primitives are passed by value, objects by reference.

A recursive function calls itself with a smaller input until it hits a BASE CASE. Types: direct, indirect (mutual), tail, head, linear, tree (e.g. Fibonacci) and nested (f(f(n))). Too-deep recursion throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded.

Every variable has a declared type: byte, short, int, long, float, double, char, boolean (primitives) or a class like String. int / int is integer division; cast with (double) for decimals. + concatenates as soon as a String is involved (left to right). Casting a double to int truncates. Compound assignments include an implicit cast.
lesson.code:
int a = 7, b = 2;
System.out.println(a / b);          // 3
System.out.println((double) a / b); // 3.5
System.out.println(a % b);          // 1
System.out.println("" + a + b);     // 72
System.out.println(a + b + "");     // 9
char c = 'A';
System.out.println((char) (c + 2)); // C

lesson.summary: Strings are immutable objects. Key methods: length(), charAt(i), substring(a, b), indexOf, lastIndexOf, contains, startsWith, endsWith, toUpperCase, toLowerCase, trim/strip, replace, split, repeat, isEmpty/isBlank, equals, equalsIgnoreCase, compareTo. Compare text with equals(), never ==. StringBuilder is the mutable alternative (append, insert, reverse, deleteCharAt).

lesson.summary: Arrays have a FIXED length (arr.length) and default values (0, false, null). Index from 0 to length − 1 or get ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException. java.util.Arrays: sort, toString, fill, copyOf, copyOfRange, equals, binarySearch, asList, stream. Array variables are references — use clone() to copy.

ArrayList<Integer> is a resizable list: add, add(i, x), get, set, remove(int index) vs remove(Object), size, contains, indexOf, clear, isEmpty, subList. Collections: sort, reverse, max, min, frequency, swap. List.of is immutable, Arrays.asList is fixed-size. Stack/ArrayDeque are LIFO, Queue/LinkedList FIFO.

Map<K, V>: put (returns old value), get (null if missing), getOrDefault, containsKey, remove, putIfAbsent, merge, keySet, values, entrySet. HashMap = no order, LinkedHashMap = insertion order, TreeMap = sorted keys. Set<E>: add (false if duplicate), contains, remove, size; HashSet / LinkedHashSet / TreeSet (sorted, first/last). addAll/retainAll/removeAll = union/intersection/difference.

if / else if / else — conditions must be boolean. switch (int, char, String, enum) jumps to a case and falls through until break. Ternary: cond ? a : b. && and || short-circuit. Compare Strings with equals().

for (init; condition; update), while, do-while (runs at least once) and the enhanced for (for (int x : arr)). break exits the loop, continue skips to the next iteration. The loop variable of an index loop keeps its final value if declared outside.

Use nested loops: the outer loop is the row, the inner loops print spaces and stars with System.out.print, then System.out.println() ends the row. Java 11's " ".repeat(k) builds a row in one expression.

Types: STATIC methods (belong to the class), INSTANCE methods (use an object's fields), CONSTRUCTORS, OVERLOADED methods (same name, different parameters), VARARGS (int... nums), RECURSIVE, ABSTRACT, and LAMBDAS implementing functional interfaces (Function, Predicate, Supplier, Consumer…). Java is always pass-by-value (references are copied).

A recursive method calls itself with a smaller input until a BASE CASE stops it. Types: direct, indirect (mutual), tail, head, linear, tree and nested recursion. Too-deep recursion throws StackOverflowError.

languages.name: C++
languages.tagline: Fast, powerful and close to the machine.

lesson.summary: Every variable has a type: int, long long, double, char, bool, string. int / int truncates; cast with (double) or static_cast<double>. cout prints doubles with 6 significant digits and drops trailing zeros; bools print as 1/0. char arithmetic uses character codes. Unsigned types wrap; signed overflow is undefined behaviour.
lesson.code:
int a = 7, b = 2;
cout << a / b << endl;          // 3
cout << (double) a / b << endl; // 3.5
cout << a % b << endl;          // 1
cout << 10.0 / 2 << endl;       // 5
cout << (a > b) << endl;        // 1
cout << char('A' + 2) << endl;  // C

lesson.summary: std::string is MUTABLE. size()/length(), s[i] and at(i), substr(pos, LEN), find/rfind (npos if missing), append/+=, insert, erase(pos, len), replace(pos, len, str), push_back/pop_back, empty, front/back. Compare with == and <. Convert with stoi/to_string. <algorithm> (sort, reverse, count) works on strings.

returns the char at an index with bounds checking (throws out_of_range)
returns the first index of a substring or string::npos
returns the last index of a substring or string::npos
returns the first index of ANY of the given characters
returns len characters starting at pos: substr(pos, len)
adds text at the end (modifies the string)

lesson.summary: C arrays have a fixed size. vector<int> grows: push_back, pop_back, insert/erase with iterators, size, front, back, at (checked), resize, clear. Vectors COPY on assignment. Range-for by reference (int& x) modifies elements. <algorithm>: sort, reverse, max_element, count, find, binary_search, lower_bound, unique; <numeric>: accumulate.

map<K, V> keeps keys sorted; unordered_map uses hashing (no order, faster). m[k] inserts a default (0) if missing; at(k) throws; count(k) is 1/0; find returns an iterator or end(); insert does not overwrite. Iterate with for (auto& [k, v] : m). pair/tuple group values; structured bindings unpack them.

set keeps unique sorted values (insert, erase, count, find, lower_bound, begin/rbegin). multiset allows duplicates — erase(value) removes ALL copies. unordered_set is a hash set. Container adaptors: stack (LIFO: push/pop/top), queue (FIFO: push/pop/front), priority_queue (largest first), deque (both ends).

if / else if / else; any non-zero value is true. switch works on integers and chars and falls through until break. Ternary: cond ? a : b. && and || short-circuit. Beware = (assignment) vs == (comparison) inside conditions.
for (init; cond; step), while, do-while (runs at least once) and range-based for (for (int x : v)). break exits, continue skips to the next iteration.
Nested loops: the outer loop controls rows; inner loops print spaces and stars; cout << endl ends a row. string(k, '*') builds k stars in one go.

Parameter passing: by VALUE (copy), by REFERENCE (int&), by POINTER (int*). Also: default arguments, overloading, templates (generic T), inline functions, static local variables and lambdas with capture lists ([=], [&], [x], [&x]).
A recursive function calls itself on a smaller problem until a BASE CASE. Types: direct, indirect, tail, head, linear, tree and nested recursion. Deep recursion can overflow the call stack.

languages.name: SQL
languages.tagline: Talk to databases — DDL, DML, DQL, DCL & TCL.

lesson.summary: DDL (Data Definition Language) defines structure: CREATE TABLE, ALTER TABLE (ADD/RENAME/DROP COLUMN, RENAME TO), DROP TABLE, TRUNCATE TABLE. Constraints guard the data: PRIMARY KEY, FOREIGN KEY, UNIQUE, NOT NULL, CHECK, DEFAULT. (The practice engine is SQLite, which uses DELETE FROM instead of TRUNCATE.)

DML (Data Manipulation Language) changes rows: INSERT INTO … VALUES (one or many rows, or INSERT … SELECT), UPDATE … SET … WHERE, DELETE FROM … WHERE. Forgetting WHERE affects EVERY row. Upserts: INSERT OR REPLACE / ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE (MERGE in other databases).
sheet: UPDATE t SET c = v WHERE …

lesson.summary: DQL (Data Query Language) = SELECT. Choose columns (or expressions), filter rows with WHERE using =, <>, <, >, BETWEEN (inclusive), IN, LIKE (% any, _ one), IS NULL, AND/OR/NOT. DISTINCT removes duplicates. NULL is never equal to anything — use IS NULL.

ORDER BY col [ASC|DESC], extra columns break ties; NULLs sort first in SQLite. LIMIT n OFFSET m for paging (TOP / FETCH FIRST in other databases). AS creates aliases. CASE WHEN … THEN … ELSE … END builds conditional values.
lesson.code:
SELECT name, salary * 12 AS yearly,
  CASE WHEN salary >= 60000 THEN 'High' ELSE 'Normal' END AS band
FROM emp
ORDER BY yearly DESC, name
LIMIT 3 OFFSET 0;

lesson.summary: COUNT(*), COUNT(col) (non-NULL only), SUM, AVG, MIN, MAX. GROUP BY produces one row per group; HAVING filters groups (WHERE filters rows before grouping). Order: SELECT … FROM … WHERE … GROUP BY … HAVING … ORDER BY … LIMIT.
lesson.code:
SELECT dept, COUNT(*) AS n, AVG(salary)
FROM emp
WHERE salary > 30000
GROUP BY dept
HAVING COUNT(*) > 1
ORDER BY dept;

lesson.summary: Combine tables on a condition: INNER JOIN (matches only), LEFT JOIN (all left rows, NULLs for no match), RIGHT JOIN, FULL OUTER JOIN, CROSS JOIN (every combination) and SELF JOIN (a table with itself via aliases).
Subqueries: scalar (one value), IN (list), EXISTS, correlated (uses the outer row), derived tables in FROM. Set operations combine results: UNION (distinct), UNION ALL, INTERSECT, EXCEPT/MINUS.

String: UPPER, LOWER, LENGTH, SUBSTR (1-based), REPLACE, TRIM, INSTR, ||. Numeric: ROUND, ABS, %, CAST. NULL handling: COALESCE, IFNULL, NULLIF. Dates (SQLite): date(d, '+7 days'), strftime('%Y', d), julianday.
lesson.code:
SELECT UPPER(name), LENGTH(city), SUBSTR(name, 1, 3),
       ROUND(salary / 12.0, 2), COALESCE(bonus, 0),
       date(joined, '+1 month')
FROM emp;

lesson.summary: TCL (Transaction Control Language): BEGIN starts a transaction, COMMIT saves it permanently, ROLLBACK undoes it, SAVEPOINT marks a point you can ROLLBACK TO. Transactions give ACID guarantees: Atomicity, Consistency, Isolation, Durability.

DCL (Data Control Language) manages permissions: GRANT privileges ON object TO user [WITH GRANT OPTION]; REVOKE privileges ON object FROM user. Privileges: SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ALL PRIVILEGES, EXECUTE. SQL commands fall into DDL, DML, DQL, DCL and TCL.

VIEW = saved query (virtual table, always current). INDEX = faster lookups (UNIQUE INDEX also blocks duplicates). Window functions compute across rows without grouping them: ROW_NUMBER, RANK, DENSE_RANK, SUM/COUNT OVER (PARTITION BY …), running totals, LAG/LEAD.
